question.text: Sanjay wishes to transfer his interest in a Category III AIF to his business associate Ritu. The Subscription Agreement restricts transfers. Which statement is correct regarding transfer restrictions in AIFs?

answer.text: AIF interests can be freely transferred like listed equity shares on a stock exchange
SEBI prohibits all transfers of AIF interests under any circumstances
Transfers are typically restricted and require prior consent of the fund manager and/or trustee, compliance with SEBI regulations, and may be subject to right of first refusal by existing investors
Transfer is automatically permitted after a 1-year lock-in period for all AIF categories

explanation.text: The Logic: AIF interests are illiquid by design and the underlying subscription documents and SEBI framework heavily restrict secondary transfers. Transfers typically require prior consent of the fund manager and/or trustee, compliance with SEBI's eligibility/minimum-investment norms, and may be subject to a right of first refusal in favour of existing investors. They are not freely tradable on an exchange, are not blanket-banned by SEBI, and there is no universal one-year auto-transfer rule. The Trap: The lock-in option seems reasonable because lock-in periods exist, but even after lock-in, transfer restrictions and consent requirements remain in place. Free-exchange-tradability and blanket-prohibition options misstate the regulatory position. Note: The specific claim that AIF-unit transfers require manager/trustee consent and may be subject to right-of-first-refusal by existing investors is not explicitly laid out in the cited workbook chapter (Series XIX-A_AIF (Category I and II) Distributors_Dec-version PDF.pdf, pp. 68, 72, 151-152, 190, 355), which discusses ROFR/ROFO in investee-company shareholder agreements rather than AIF-unit transfers. The framing above is general industry practice for AIF Subscription Agreements.
